newsitem.title: USA: Amazon Indians meet to save rainforest habitat.
newsitem.headline: Amazon Indians meet to save rainforest habitat.

text.p: Thirty Amazon Indian leaders gathered in the U.S. capital on Wednesday to campaign for the preservation of their rainforest habitat threatened by gold miners, lumberjacks, oil companies and disease.

Among them were representatives of the Yanomami, the last major primitive tribe left in the Amazon, who said their lands on Brazil's border with Venezuela are once again being invaded by gold prospectors.

The Indian leaders from eight Amazon basin nations will lobby U.S. officials for support and work on a two-year plan to protect their environment. They will have meetings with the U.S. State Department, the World Bank, the Organisation of American States and California Democrat Tom Lantos, co-chairman of the Congressional Human Rights Caucus.
The four-day forum was organised by the Amazon Coalition, a Washington-based alliance of environmentalists and human rights workers striving to save the Amazon and its native peoples.
"We are asking for the demarcation of our lands to ensure the survival of our societies," said Washington Bolivar Diaz, of the Cashibo-Cacataibo tribe in Peru's Amazon jungle.
"We are guardians of the world's lungs because we know how to look after the rainforest," he said in an interview.
Diaz said oil, logging and gold mining companies are entering the Peruvian Amazon without consulting its native peoples, polluting rivers and poisoning the fish.

He said President Alberto Fujimori's government had curtailed native rights in changes to Peru's constitution and was breaking international agreements by allowing companies to tap jungle resources without contacting the local Indians.

In Brazil, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's government has been dragging its feet on promises to expel wildcat miners from Yanomami lands, Claudia Andujar, coordinator of the Pro-Yanomami Commission (CCPY), said.

Her non-profit group succeeded in getting Brazil to create a Yanomami native reserve the size of Portugal in 1991, legally protecting 36,000 square miles (94,000 sq kms) of jungle where most of the Brazilian Yanomami live.
This has not stopped the invasion by "garimpeiros" (wildcat miners), bringing in illnesses, prostitution, guns and death.
In August 1993, miners reportedly massacred a Yanomami village on the banks of the Haximu river, killing 16 men, women and children and decapitating some of them with machetes.
The Yanomami are the last large unacculturated group of people on Earth living much the same way that Europeans encountered the first Americans 500 years ago.
Their numbers have dwindled to about 9,000 on the Brazilian side and 11,000 in Venezuela. They have managed to retain their culture due to their isolation in a remote corner of Amazonia.
But venereal disease, hepatitis, tuberculosis, flu and malaria have taken their toll.
"There are an estimated 3,000 miners inside the reserve today," Andujar said. "The government set aside $6 million to expel them, but no one knows where the money went. It just disappeared."
Andujar, a photo-journalist whose work led her to dedicate her energy to defending the Yanomami, said malaria introduced by the miners is the number one killer.
But the guns and bullets the miners have traded are also lethal, encouraging infighting between tribes that has taken 12 Yanomami lives in the last year, she said.

Brazil's government could easily destroy the 24 clandestine airstrips built by miners on Yanomami land and stop their planes flying in, but it is unwilling to do so because President Cardoso needs the support of local Roraima State politicians to secure his re-election, Andujar said.
"This is not a good moment to be an Indian in Brazil," she said. "The country is pursuing neo-liberal economic policies that favour business interests."
